title: Serial vs. Serializable: Interleaving Is Allowed
misconception: Confusing serializable with serial: believing a serializable schedule cannot interleave operations, when it only needs to be equivalent to some serial schedule.

transcript.text: Two words get mixed up. A serial schedule runs each transaction as one contiguous block. A serializable schedule only has to leave the database in the same state as some serial schedule.
Look at S5. Transaction 2's read of x lands in the middle of transaction 1's operations, so this schedule is interleaved and is not serial.

Now compare it with S6, a serial schedule, where T2's read comes after all of T1. S5 has the same reads-from and the same final writes as S6. So S5 is view-equivalent to a serial schedule, and that makes it serializable.
So interleaving does not break serializability. What matters is that the outcome matches some serial order. Now try a new question yourself and ask: does the result match a serial schedule?

jury.reason: All claims are supported by the cited pages. Serial is defined as contiguous per transaction (p.19), serializable as leaving the database in the same state as some serial schedule (p.20). S5 is correctly identified as interleaved, and S6 is correctly identified as serial and view-equivalent to S5 (p.22, p.24). The highlight indices point to the correct operations (r2(x) in both schedules). The citation quotes appear verbatim on their stated pages. The script teaches the concept without naming, pointing to, or grading any quiz option, and the output is in English.
